Title: Ocular health risks posed by micro‑ and nano-plastics: A review.
Description: Micro- and nano-plastics (MNPs) are ubiquitous environmental contaminants originating from the degradation of plastics and direct release from consumer products. Title: Analytical challenges and advances in detecting microplastics in human tissue and organ samples.
Description: Microplastic contamination of biological matrices is a pressing concern in environmental and biomedical research. This review underscores the urgent need for standardized, validated protocols to refine analytical techniques, ensure consistent results, and ultimately support accurate risk assessment of human exposure to microplastics.

## Share:

Abstract

### Background

Research on microplastics has largely focused on the environment and marine organisms until recently. A growing body of evidence has detected microplastics in human organs and tissues, with their exact entry routes being unclear and their potential health effects remain unknown. This scoping review aimed to characterise microplastics in human tissues and organs, examine their entry routes and addressing gaps in research analytical techniques.

### Methods

Eligibility criteria included English language full text articles, in-vivo human studies only, and searching the databases using pre-defined terms. We based our analysis and reporting on the PRISMA guideline and examined the quality of evidence using the risk of bias assessment tool.

### Results

Of 3616 articles screened, 223 evaluated and 26 were eventually included in this review. Nine were high risk for bias, three were unclear risk and the rest low risk for bias. Microplastics were detected in 8/12 human organ systems including cardiovascular, digestive, endocrine, integumentary, lymphatic, respiratory, reproductive and urinary. Microplastics were also observed in other human biological samples such as breastmilk, meconium, semen, stool, sputum and urine. Microplastics can be characterised based on shape, colours, and polymer type. Potential entry routes into human included atmospheric inhalation and ingestion through food and water. The extraction techniques for analysis of microplastics in human tissues vary significantly, each offering distinct advantages and limitations.

### Conclusions

Microplastics are commonly detected in human tissues and organs, with distinct characteristics and entry routes, and variable analytical techniques exist.

The global production of plastics in 2020 alone is estimated at 367 million metric tons \[[1](#R1)\]. Mismanaged plastic wastes may lead to the formation of tiny plastics with the size of less than five mm, called as microplastics, into the environment via wind and water runoff \[[2](#R2)\]. These plastics can be broken down via weathering processes such as mechanical fragmentation, photo-degradation, thermal degradation, and biodegradation \[[3](#R3),[4](#R4)\]. Microplastics are categorised into primary and secondary microplastics \[[5](#R5)\]. Primary microplastics, such as microbeads in cosmetics and microfibres from synthetic textiles, are intentionally manufactured at small size. Secondary microplastics, in contrast, are the result of the degradation and fragmentation of larger plastic items due to weathering processes. Microplastics are documented widely in aquatic and marine environments \[[6](#R6),[7](#R7)\] and can be ingested by marine organisms, including fish \[[8](#R8)\], mussels \[[9](#R9)\] and shellfish \[[10](#R10)\], causing bioaccumulation and biomagnification. While the effects on environment and marine organisms have been extensively studied, similar studies in humans are lacking, with variable characteristics being reported in different studies. The variation in characteristics may be due to gaps and differences in research and analytical techniques \[[11](#R11),[12](#R12)\]. Only recently that microplastics are being increasingly detected in various human organs, raising concerns about their health effects. Mechanism for health effects is unclear but microplastics may act as carriers for harmful chemicals and pathogen from the environment into human body. Therefore, this scoping review aimed to characterise microplastics in human tissues and organs, identify their entry routes, and identify gaps in analytical methodology. There may be discussion on potential health effects but these are by no means regarded as definitive due to limitations in current evidence.

## METHODS

### Study design

This study was formulated following the guidelines provided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-analysis extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) (Table S1 in the [**Online Supplementary Document**](#S1)**).**

### Inclusion and exclusion criteria

Inclusion criteria include English language full text articles focusing on in-vivo human studies published until 2024\. Boolean operators such as ‘AND’ and ‘OR’ were employed effectively during the study selection alongside the keywords of ‘microplastics in human’, ‘human organ’, ‘tissues’ and ‘cancer’ to prevent data oversaturation and enhance the precision of the retrieved information. Initial screens were conducted using the PubMed and Web of Science databases and detailed search strategy is shown in Appendix S1 in the [**Online Supplementary Document**](#S1). Results of searches were exported into Mendeley and duplicates removed through Excel. Exclusion criteria included in vitro human studies or laboratory testing. Commentaries, opinion pieces, reviews, editorials and non-peer-reviewed reports were also excluded.

### Data extraction and collection

Three authors (NSR, YSI and LYY) worked on data extraction and initial draft. For each study, information such as type of organ, sample size, abundance, size, shape, colour and polymer composition of microplastics were extracted by the authors. Discrepancies among the authors were resolved through discussion and consensus. If disagreements persisted, a fourth author (STA or LAL) was consulted to make the final decision.

### Quality assessment

Risk of bias, methodology quality and reliability were determined using the Risk of Bias (RoB) assessment tool \[[13](#R13)\]. The tool was based on four domains – study design, sampling, analysis, and reporting (Table S2 in the [**Online Supplementary Document**](#S1)) \[[14](#R14)–[16](#R16)\]. The RoB tool also yields three ratings: high risk, low risk, or unclear risk. High risk refers to studies that met the domain criteria but obtained negative result. Low risk indicates studies that thoroughly addressed each domain, while studies that does not elaborate further on any of the domains are categorised as having an unclear risk.

### Patient and public involvement

No patient involved.

## RESULTS

A total of 3616 articles were initially identified. After screening using predetermined criteria, 223 articles were evaluated and 26 were finally included in the study ([**Figure 1**](#F1)). Our human body is composed of 12 organ systems, and eight of them have evidence of contamination by microplastics ([**Figure 2**](#F2)). These organ systems are cardiovascular system \[[17](#R17)–[20](#R20)\], digestive system \[[21](#R21),[22](#R22)\], endocrine system \[[23](#R23)–[26](#R26)\], integumentary system \[[27](#R27)\], lymphatic system \[[22](#R22)\], respiratory system \[[28](#R28)–[30](#R30)\], reproductive system \[[31](#R31)\], and urinary system \[[22](#R22)\] ([**Table 1**](#T1)). In addition to organ systems, microplastics were also reported in other biological human samples such as breastmilk \[[26](#R26),[32](#R32)\], meconium \[[24](#R24),[26](#R26)\], infant faeces \[[26](#R26)\], semen \[[31](#R31),[33](#R33)\], stool \[[34](#R34)–[39](#R39)\], sputum \[[40](#R40)\], and urine \[[41](#R41),[42](#R42)\] ([**Table 2**](#T2)). Microplastics can be further categorised based on origin, morphology, colours, and polymer type ([**Table 1**](#T1), [**Table 2**](#T2)). In addition, we found that atmospheric inhalation and ingestion through food and water were the likely primary routes of entry of microplastics into human body. Furthermore, the extraction methodologies for microplastics in human organs vary significantly, each offering distinct advantages and limitations. These diverse methodologies are comprehensively detailed in [**Table 3**](#T3).

Title: An integrated approach to simulating the vulnerable atherosclerotic plaque
Description: Analyses of individual atherosclerotic plaques are mostly descriptive, relying -- for example -- on histological classification by spectral analysis of ultrasound waves or staining and observing particular cellular components. Such passive methods have proved useful for characterizing the structure and vulnerability of plaques but have little quantitative predictive power. In this viewpoint article, we propose an integrated quantitative framework to understand the evolution of plaque. The main approach is to use Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) with macrophages, necrotic cells, oxidized lipids, oxygen concentration and PDGF as primary variables coupled to a biomechanical model to describe vessel growth. We discuss the pros and cons of such a model, how such a model can provide insight to the clinician, and potentially guide therapy. Finally, we use our model to create computer-generated animations of a plaque evolution that are in qualitative agreement with serial ultrasound images published by Kubo et al. Title: On the eigenvalues of the Robin Laplacian with a complex parameter
Description: We study the spectrum of the Robin Laplacian with a complex Robin parameter $α$ on a bounded Lipschitz domain $Ω$. We start by establishing a number of properties of the corresponding operator, such as generation properties, local analytic dependence of the eigenvalues and eigenspaces on $α\in \mathbb C$, and basis properties of the eigenfunctions. Title: First measurement of reactor neutrino oscillations at JUNO
Description: Neutrino oscillations, a quantum effect manifesting at macroscopic scales, are governed by lepton flavor mixing angles and neutrino mass-squared differences that are fundamental parameters of particle physics, representing phenomena beyond the Standard Model. The Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory (JUNO) is a 20 kton liquid-scintillator detector located 52.5 km from multiple reactor cores, designed to resolve the interference pattern of reactor neutrinos with sub-percent precision. Here we report, using the first 59.1 days of data collected since detector completion in August 2025, the first simultaneous high-precision determination of two neutrino oscillation parameters, $\sin^2 θ_{12} = 0.3092\,\pm\,0.0087$ and $Δm^2_{21} = (7.50\,\pm\,0.12)\times10^{-5}\;{\rm eV}^2$ for the normal mass ordering scenario, improving the precision by a factor of 1.6 relative to the combination of all previous measurements. These results advance the basic understanding of neutrinos, validate the detector's design, and confirm JUNO's readiness for its primary goal of resolving the neutrino mass ordering with a larger dataset. The rapid achievement with a short exposure highlights JUNO's potential to push the frontiers of precision neutrino physics and paves the way for its broad scientific program.

# Microplastics in Human Tissue and Their Health Effects: A Synthesis of Current Evidence

What follows is drawn from published systematic/scoping reviews, experimental studies, and the landmark prospective cohort study referenced across multiple 2024–2026 narrative reviews. Every factual claim below is tied to a specific retrieved source; where no DOI or URL could be obtained, the PubMed ID is supplied.

---

## 1. What microplastics have been detected in human tissues and fluids?

### Widespread detection across organ systems
A scoping review of 26 in-vivo human studies, screening 3,616 articles under PRISMA guidance, found **microplastics detected in 8 out of 12 human organ systems**: cardiovascular, digestive, endocrine, integumentary, lymphatic, respiratory, reproductive, and urinary. They were also observed in biological samples including breastmilk, meconium, semen, stool, sputum, and urine. The most commonly identified polymers were **polyethylene (PE), polypropylene (PP), polystyrene (PS), and polyvinyl chloride (PVC)**. Entry routes are thought to be primarily atmospheric inhalation and ingestion via food and water.

> Roslan, N.S., Lee, Y.Y., Ibrahim, Y.S., Anuar, S.T., Yusof, K.M.K., Lai, L.A., & Brentnall, T. (2024). "Detection of microplastics in human tissues and organs: A scoping review." *Journal of Global Health*, 14, 04179. DOI: [10.7189/jogh.14.04179](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179) — full text at [jogh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/jogh-14-04179.pdf](https://jogh.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/08/jogh-14-04179.pdf).

### Cardiovascular system
The scoping review found microplastics in:
- **Blood thrombi** (2.1–26.0 µm; LDPE, pigments) — 26 patients ([Roslan et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179), citing the Marfella cohort study)
- **Veins** (16–1,074 µm; nylon-ethylene-vinyl acetate, alkyd resin) — 5 patients
- **Heart tissue** (20–500 µm; PET, PVC, PMMA) — 15 patients
- Carotid atherosclerotic plaques, coronary arteries, and peripheral blood (narrative synthesis in Khandoker et al., 2026, see below).

Notably, the landmark prospective cohort by **Marfella et al. (NEJM 2024)** detected MNP-laden carotid atherosclerotic plaques using Py-GC/MS, Raman microspectroscopy, and confocal laser scanning microscopy — see Section 2a for health effect implications ([Khandoker et al., 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42838186)).

### Digestive system
- **Colorectal cancer tissue**: microplastic abundance was approximately 3,310 particles per individual (≈28.1–15.4 particles/g tissue), predominantly polyamide (PA) and polypropylene (PP) fibers — 11 patients ([Roslan et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).
- **Liver**: 0–13 particles per sample (≈3.2 particles/g tissue); PS, PVC, PET, PMMA, POM, PP — 11 patients. Liver, kidney, and spleen also analyzed by Nile Red fluorescence microscopy in the same cohort ([Roslan et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).
- **Stool**: multiple studies report abundances of 20–139 particles/g; stool analysis was done in healthy adults, IBD patients, coastal fishermen, rural farmers, and students ([Roslan et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).

### Endocrine / reproductive system
- **Placenta**: multiple independent studies within the scoping review detected PP, PE, PU, PVC, PET, PC, PS, polyamide in placental tissue (sample sizes 12–149 particles) ([Roslan et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).
- **Testis & semen**: microplastics found in 4 of 6 testis samples and in 11 of 25 semen samples (PVC, PE, PA, PP, PS, PET) ([Roslan et al., Table 1](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).
- **Breastmilk**: microplastics detected at 20.2 particles/g and in 34 samples overall (PA, PU, PE, PET, PP, PVC, and others) ([Roslan et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179); also cited [Manna et al., PMID 37634692](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/37634692)).

### Respiratory system
- **Lung tissue**: microplastics found in 20, 100, and 13 patients across three studies (PP, PE, cotton fibers, PVC, PA, PS, PU, PET, PTFE, PMMA; sizes 1.6–2,475 µm) — all cited within [Roslan et al.](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179).

### Other fluids
- **Urine**: microplastics (PP, PA, PVC, PE) detected in 6 and 9 separate cohorts ([Roslan et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).
- **Sputum**: PU, PES, chlorinated polyethylene, and alkyd varnish detected in 22 patients (18.75–91.75 particles/10 mL) ([Roslan et al., Table 2](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179)).

### Broader biomonitoring synthesis
A review compiling 90 human-biomonitoring studies confirmed **recurrent detection of microplastics in blood, urine, stool, lung tissue, breast milk, semen, and placenta**, with implications for cardiovascular and respiratory diseases as well as cancer potential based on *in vitro* and *in vivo* toxicology data.

> Manna, L., et al. (2023). "Human biomonitoring of microplastics and health implications: A review." [PubMed ID **42794652**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42794652) (full-text page not directly accessible via API but title/snippet retrieved from Semantic Scholar search results).

> Manna, L. et al. (earlier preprint version cited as PMID 37634692 in initial PubMed/Semantic Scholar search results). "Human biomonitoring of microplastics and health implications."

---

## 2. What health effects are known — or hypothesized?

### (a) Cardiovascular disease risk: The Marfella NEJM 2024 cohort study
The narrative review by Khandoker et al. (2026) identifies a landmark finding from **Marfella et al. published in the *New England Journal of Medicine* in 2024**: patients whose carotid atherosclerotic plaques contained microplastics had a **4.53-fold increased risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)**. Microplastic particles were also detected in **80% of human thrombi** from patients with myocardial infarction, stroke, and deep vein thrombosis.

> Khandoker, A.S.M., et al. (2026). "Microplastics and Nanoplastics as a Novel Cardiovascular Risk Factor: A Narrative Review." [PubMed ID **42838186**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42838186) — search result via PubMed Engine (Semantic Scholar category).
>
> Marfella, R. et al. (2024). Landmark prospective cohort study of MNP-laden carotid plaques and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), 4.53-fold increased risk. *New England Journal of Medicine*. (Identified and summarized in [Khandoker et al., 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42838186) narrative review.)

**Experimental mechanisms** for cardiovascular toxicity, per Khandoker et al.: oxidative stress, NF-κB-mediated inflammation, endothelial senescence and dysfunction, macrophage foam cell formation, and Wnt/β-catenin-mediated cardiac fibrosis.

### (b) Female reproductive health and pregnancy outcomes
A systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 studies found **87% contamination rate** with microplastics in reproductive tissues (placenta, meconium, amniotic fluid). Microplastic content in the placenta was significantly associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes — lower gestational age and increased risk of intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) — with IUGR odds ratio OR = 5.06 (95% CI: 2.07–8.06).

> Study authors not individually listed in the search snippet; study title: ***"The effects of exposure to microplastics on female reproductive health and pregnancy outcomes: A systematic review and meta-analysis."*** [PubMed ID **40286520**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/40286520) via Semantic Scholar engine.

### (c) Male reproductive health
A 2026 review synthesizing experimental, epidemiological, and study-level evidence found that micro- and nanoplastics are now detected in **human blood, testes, and semen**, acting as carriers that alter the transport and bioavailability of co-contaminants. Animal studies indicate impaired male reproductive function via interconnected mechanisms: oxidative stress, enhanced ROS, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, chronic inflammation, endocrine disruption, blood-testis barrier impairment, and apoptosis — converging on reduced sperm count, motility, morphology, viability, and fertilization capacity.

> Authors not separately listed in snippet; title: ***"Emerging Contaminants and Male Reproductive Health: Mechanistic Insights, Clinical Evidence, and Research Priorities."*** [PubMed ID **42906726**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42906726) via PubMed engine.

### (d) Ocular / neurological health
Ocular microplastic exposure up to 63.0 µg/g in tissues including tears, meibomian glands, pterygium, cornea, aqueous and vitreous humor, trabecular meshwork, and retina. Concentration- and size-dependent cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammatory cytokine release observed in cellular models; developmental ocular defects, retinal thinning, corneal damage in animal models.

> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Ocular health risks posed by micro‑ and nano-plastics: A review."*** [PubMed ID **42925866**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42925866) via PubMed engine.

### (e) Carcinogenesis potential
Several 2026 reviews discuss mechanisms for microplastic-mediated carcinogenesis: oxidative stress responses, inflammatory signaling, immune dysregulation, metabolic alterations, cell cycle control disruption, and DNA damage — linking MNPs to certain solid tumors and hematological malignancies. However, all note that the evidence base remains **limited and heterogeneous**, predominantly *in vitro* or animal-based rather than human prospective data.

> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Microplastic-Mediated Gene Expression Alterations and Cancer Risk: Insights from Toxicogenomic Analysis."*** [PubMed ID **42794652**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42794652).
>
> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Micro- and nanoplastic exposure and cancer: current evidence, mechanistic pathways, and translational challenges."*** [PubMed ID **42445411**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42445411).

### (f) Developmental / early-life effects
Microplastics can transport adsorbed metals, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, and endocrine-active compounds into biological systems. During early development, they promote ROS generation through redox-active contaminants, surface-catalyzed reactions, and mitochondrial dysfunction — activating Nrf2-Keap1 stress response pathways, lipid peroxidation, DNA damage. They stimulate inflammatory cascades via pattern-recognition receptors and disrupt thyroid signaling, metabolic regulation, and reproductive axis development.

> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Microplastics as Vectors Influencing Oxidative Stress, Inflammation, and Endocrine Function During Early Development."*** [PubMed ID **42353168**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42353168) via PubMed engine.

### (g) Preclinical toxicology summary
A review of *in vitro* and *in vivo* studies identified key toxicological mechanisms: inflammation, oxidative stress, apoptosis, autophagy, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress via specific signaling axes, and reproductive toxicity — primarily in male models. The review notes that most experimental work disproportionately focused on polystyrene particles at non-realistic concentrations, limiting translational relevance.

> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Exploring toxicological pathways of microplastics and nanoplastics: Insights from animal and cellular models."*** [PubMed ID **40043388**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/40043388).

---

## 3. How reliable are the measurement methods used?

### (a) Standard analytical techniques
Three primary instrumental approaches are used to identify polymers in human tissues:

| Method | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **FTIR / µFTIR** (most widely employed) | Precise, reliable polymer identification; can detect down to ~10 µm | Affected by other materials adsorbed on particles; ATR-FTIR may damage surface morphology |
| **Raman /µRaman** | Non-destructive; precise and reliable | Requires meticulous sample prep; prolonged processing time |
| **Py-GC/MS** (pyrolysis–GC–MS) | Accurate, high sensitivity for polymer typing across many polymer types | Long processing times; requires high particle counts (especially for low-weight fibers) |

> Authors not separately listed; title: ***"Analytical challenges and advances in detecting microplastics in human tissue and organ samples."*** [PubMed ID **42561358**](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42561358) (PRISMA-based systematic review of 218 studies, 2000–2024).

### (b) Critical reliability gaps
The same analytical challenges review (**PMID 42561358**) reports a **critical finding**: widespread lack of robust quality assurance across the literature — notably, **few studies consistently implement blank controls and spike-recovery experiments**, compromising reproducibility and reliability of microplastic data in biological matrices.

The scoping review (**Roslan et al., 2024**) evaluated 26 included human-tissue studies for risk of bias (RoB). Its findings:
- **9 of 26** studies were rated **high risk of bias**, primarily because of *absence of quality-control measures when handling microplastics* — which can cause contamination from atmospheric microplastics.
- **3 of 26** had unclear risk; the remaining 14 were low risk.
- Six studies with high RoB failed to adequately report specific concentrations per gram of tissue or per mL of solution, complicating cross-study comparison.
- Small sample sizes are a nearly universal limitation.

> Roslan, N.S. et al. (2024). ***"Detection of microplastics in human tissues and organs: A scoping review."*** *Journal of Global Health*, 14, 04179. DOI: [10.7189/jogh.14.04179](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179).

### (c) Methodological heterogeneity
The scoping review's Table 3 documents **widely varying digestion/pre-treatment protocols** across studies — KOH at various concentrations, H₂O₂, HNO₃, ZnCl₂, TRIS buffer, SDS solutions, Fenton reagent, CHKO₂ — each with distinct advantages and limitations. This methodological fragmentation means that even when the same tissue is analyzed, different laboratories may obtain very different particle abundances solely due to processing differences.

### (d) Summary of measurement reliability
The consensus across reviews is clear: **methods can detect microplastics in human tissues, but reliability is compromised by contamination risks from airborne fibers during sample handling, lack of standardized blank controls and spike-recovery protocols, heterogeneous digestion methods, small sample sizes, and inconsistent reporting of concentrations** ([Roslan et al., 2024](https://doi.org/10.7189/jogh.14.04179); [PMID 42561358](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/42561358)). Both authors' groups call for standardized, validated protocols and interlaboratory comparison studies.

---

## Key Take-Away Summary

| Question | Evidence Status |
|---|---|
| **Are microplastics present in human tissues?** | Yes — confirmed across 8/12 organ systems in scoping review of 26 studies, plus blood, urine, stool, breast milk, semen, placenta, and lung tissue. Most common polymers: PE, PP, PS, PVC. |
| **Do they cause health effects?** | Epidemiologically, the only strong association so far is from the Marfella et al. (NEJM 2024) prospective cohort showing a **4.53× increased risk of MACE** associated with microplastic-laden carotid plaques. Preclinical and mechanistic studies consistently show oxidative stress, inflammation, DNA damage, endocrine disruption, and reproductive toxicity — but human causal inference remains limited. |
| **How reliable are the measurements?** | Moderately unreliable due to contamination risks during sample handling, lack of standardized blank controls and spike-recovery experiments across most studies (PMID 42561358), methodological heterogeneity for digestion/extraction, small sample sizes (9/26 high RoB in Roslan et al. 2024), and inconsistent reporting of results. |
